Remove every complete single-line Markdown link text and every bare URL beginning with   or  deleting the full link construct rather than retaining its label or URL. Delete every ` character everywhere, including code delimiters; remove #, * and - everywhere except inside the contents of inline code spans and fenced code blocks, whose contents must otherwise remain unchanged after their backtick delimiters are removed. Remove all matches on a line, remove only the inner link in nested forms such as [text] and any resulting empty [], do not match links across line breaks, preserve all other original characters including whitespace and line breaks exactly, and output only the sanitized text with no commentary or wrapper formatting. :

Strongest non-obvious approach: separate “intent latency” from “inference latency” with a two-phase, snapshot-backed session—not a permanently warm GPU.

1. Snapshot only the immutable serving substrate

Use a deployed Modal Class with both CPU and GPU snapshots, and put imports, model load, CUDA context creation, tokenizer/template setup, kernel compilation, allocator setup, and a tiny representative forward pass in @modal.enter(snap=True). Modal explicitly recommends GPU warmup before snapshotting, and reports that snapshots can reduce cold starts by about 10×; however, it warns that snapshots often do not help when weight loading dominates, and may add overhead. Memory Snapshots | Modal DocsHigh-performance LLM inference

After restore, use @modal.enter(snap=False) only for cheap, mutable activation: create the request queue, health state, stream plumbing, and a small initial cache. Modal’s own snapshot example starts the server and warms it before the snapshot, then wakes it after restoration. Memory Snapshots | Modal DocsLow Latency, Serverless LFM2 with vLLM and Modal

The key design decision is not to snapshot a 131,072-token KV cache. Snapshot the model and execution substrate, but defer the large request cache until after restore. This minimizes snapshot dirty pages and restore transfer while retaining the expensive CUDA/JIT/model initialization work.

2. ExLlamaV3: treat max_num_tokens as a capacity reservation, not context length

ExLlamaV3’s Cache constructor defines max_num_tokens as total capacity across concurrent jobs, and requires a multiple of 256; for dynamic generation it is the aggregate token budget, not necessarily one sequence’s context window. exllamav3/cache/cache.py at cb1a436f · turboderp-org/exllamav3 CacheLayer_quant initially holds no tensors, but alloc creates qk, qv, sk, and sv with torch.zeros on the GPU. exllamav3/cache/quant.py at cb1a436f · turboderp-org/exllamav3 Therefore, constructing Cache is cheap, while allocating it is the VRAM/snapshot event.

At 131,072 tokens, allocating every layer’s quantized cache before snapshot creates a large GPU allocation and—because zeros writes the allocation—touches pages that the snapshot must preserve. The practical configuration is:

- Model snapshot: no full Cache.alloc before snap.
- Post-restore cache: allocate a conservative multiple of 256, based on observed concurrency and prompt lengths, not the model’s advertised maximum context.
- Grow capacity in page increments or recreate the cache when a long-context request actually arrives.
- Use quantized KV settings such as k_bits=4/ v_bits=4 or 8/8 only after measuring quality; lower bits reduce footprint but do not make the allocation free.
- Keep max_num_tokens equal to a measured service budget, for example max concurrent requests × expected active tokens plus headroom, rather than 131072 by default.

This follows directly from the implementation: CacheLayer_quant computes page-shaped q/k/v/scale tensors from max_num_tokens and allocates all four with torch.zeros; its dequantized temporary K/V tensors are separately created during get_kv. exllamav3/cache/quant.py at cb1a436f · turboderp-org/exllamav3 Consequently, reducing max_num_tokens reduces both resident KV memory and the amount of memory that can be dirtied during warmup. The loader also creates temporary quantized-cache placeholders to account for dequantization overhead, so VRAM profiling must include transient peaks, not just final cache size. exllamav3/model/model_ls.py at cb1a436f · turboderp-org/exllamav3

Do not “prevent touching” the buffer by merely using torch.empty if the inference path later requires initialized values: uninitialized memory is unsafe. If a code change is acceptable, implement genuinely paged/lazy CacheLayer_quant allocation: allocate only the first pages, zero each page immediately before first use, and return pages to a pool after a request. That is the strongest reduction, but it requires auditing PageTable, update_kv, dequant_cache_paged, and concurrency locking. The existing generator is already page-oriented and derives capacity from the page table, which makes this direction more natural than a monolithic static cache. exllamav3/generator/generator.py

3. Dynamic context is a latency/memory trade-off, not a free optimization

Use a short-context model configuration for ordinary requests where the model supports dynamic RoPE selection, while retaining a separate long-context deployment/configuration for requests that genuinely need 131k. ExLlamaV3 exposes override_dynamic_seq_len specifically to select positional-embedding/RoPE behavior when the expected maximum context is known. exllamav3/model_init.py at cb1a436f · turboderp-org/exllamav3 Do not claim that this alone shrinks KV allocation: it only changes model configuration; max_num_tokens still controls cache capacity.

Benchmark four independently: model load, Cache.alloc, first prefill, and first decode. Record torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated/reserved, allocation latency, first-token latency, and snapshot/restore latency at 4k/32k/131k. This will identify whether the real bottleneck is weights, cache zeroing, temporary dequantization, or first-use kernels.

4. Storage hierarchy: bake software, persist weights, use local scratch only as a staging optimization

Bake immutable Python/CUDA libraries and small metadata into the image. Put multi-GB EXL3 weights in a Modal Volume unless an empirical test proves the image is faster for this exact artifact. Modal recommends Volumes for model weights and says performance is similar to image storage, while Volumes are more flexible; image changes can trigger rebuild/download work from the changed layer. model-weights.md

On first container entry, copy the EXL3 files from the Volume to local SSD scratch, verify a manifest, and load from scratch only if ExLlama’s loader benefits from local reads. This removes repeated remote reads within the container, but it cannot eliminate the first copy. Modal documents Volume read rates around 1–2 GB/s, roughly a second per GB, so a 20–30 GB model still has an irreducible multi-second storage phase unless it is included in the captured resident state. High-performance LLM inference

The decisive caveat is that GPU snapshots do not magically solve weight I/O: Modal explicitly says they generally do not improve—and can worsen—cold starts when most initialization time is weight loading. Memory Snapshots | Modal Docs Measure Volume versus image layers versus local SSD on the target GPU/region; choose based on p50/p95, not assumptions. Do not use a Volume as a live mutable filesystem without handling its explicit reload/commit semantics. Volume

5. Zero-idle-cost routing pattern

Use a cheap always-on CPU edge/gateway, not a GPU keep-warm replica:

- On page focus, route change, conversation-open, document upload completion, or a 250–500 ms typing debounce, send a signed “intent/prefetch” event.
- The gateway invokes the snapshot-backed GPU function asynchronously with a short TTL and a deduplication key. It does not send speculative GPU tokens unless the user has crossed a high-confidence intent threshold.
- The browser immediately opens/holds the streaming request or HTTP/2 stream and displays “preparing context”; the edge buffers no unbounded data.
- On the real submit, route by session ID to the restoring/ready container, reuse any prefetched prompt-prefix KV state if available, and stream the first token immediately.
- Cancel prefetch on blur, navigation, or changed prompt; never pay for speculative generation.
- Use a tiered fallback: cached answer/prefix or CPU response first; snapshot GPU for normal requests; an optional higher-latency long-context path only when the prompt exceeds the short-context budget.

Modal’s server architecture already includes a streaming edge proxy, stateless proxy, and compute load balancer, and HTTP/2 pooling/multiplexing reduces connection overhead. Modal's serverless Servers A held client connection can hide queue/restore time, but it cannot make GPU restoration instantaneous; it is a UX mask, not a compute optimization.

6. Critique and correction

The weak version of this plan would call enable_gpu_snapshot=True, allocate and fully warm a 131k cache, and assume restore is free. That is likely self-defeating: it maximizes GPU dirty state, consumes VRAM needed for weights and temporary dequantization, and snapshots work Modal says is least likely to benefit when weight I/O dominates. Memory Snapshots | Modal Docsexllamav3/cache/quant.py at cb1a436f · turboderp-org/exllamav3exllamav3/model/model_ls.py at cb1a436f · turboderp-org/exllamav3

The corrected strongest plan is therefore a “small immutable snapshot + post-restore paged cache + intent-triggered activation” architecture. It achieves zero incremental idle GPU billing only when no GPU is activated; once intent causes a container to start, GPU seconds are necessarily billable. No architecture can simultaneously guarantee zero idle cost, zero speculative GPU cost, and zero cold-start latency. The honest objective is zero standby GPU cost and masked TTFT for high-probability interactions, with a measured short-context fast path and an explicitly slower 131k path.

Recommended acceptance tests: p95 intent-to-ready, submit-to-first-token, GPU billed seconds per session, snapshot byte size, restore page-fault time, Volume-to-scratch throughput, cache allocation time, peak reserved VRAM, and cancellation waste. Ship the design only if prefetch cancellation keeps wasted GPU seconds below the cost/latency threshold and if snapshotting the model substrate beats a no-snapshot baseline on the actual EXL3 model and GPU.
